message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and responsibilities that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and federal law. For specific situations—especially those involving disputes, evictions, or health and safety concerns—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a security deposit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written move‑in checklist.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the deposit is withheld. | | **Habitability / Repairs** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and habitable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• The landlord must repair any major defects within a reasonable time after notice. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Increases** | • Landlords may raise rent **only at the end of a lease term** or with proper notice (30 days for month‑to‑month, 60 days for longer leases).
• No “rent‑control” laws exist in Texas. | • Review your lease for the notice period.
• Negotiate or contest unreasonable increases if you believe they violate the lease terms. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants can terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• Tenants who have a fixed‑term lease may terminate early only if the lease allows it or if the landlord breaches the lease. | • Provide written notice to the landlord.
• Keep copies of all correspondence. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Property Code §92.001–92.006**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• Eviction can only proceed after a court order. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend any court hearing; you can present evidence of payment or lease compliance. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords may enter only for **reasonable purposes** (repairs, inspections, showing to prospective tenants) and must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** (unless emergency). | • Keep a log of all entries.
• If entry is unreasonably frequent or without notice, you can file a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected classes: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, age, etc.
• Landlords cannot refuse to rent or impose different terms based on these characteristics. | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Health & Safety** | • Landlords must comply with local building codes, fire codes, and health regulations.
• Tenants can report violations to local health or building departments. | • Document violations (photos, dates).
• Request a written response from the landlord. | | **Utilities** | • Landlords may require tenants to pay utilities, but must provide a written statement of which utilities are included. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Tenants may sublet or assign the lease only if the lease permits or with landlord’s written consent. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Remedies** | • If the landlord breaches the lease, you may:
 • Seek damages in small‑claims court (up to $20,000).
 • Request specific performance (e.g., repair).
 • Terminate the lease and move out. | • Keep all documentation (receipts, notices, emails).
• Consider mediation before litigation. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand rent amount, due dates, security deposit limits, pet policies, and notice requirements. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you in disputes. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 30 days for month‑to‑month termination, 60 days for longer leases, 24‑hour notice for entry. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Write a clear, dated notice to the landlord. Follow up in writing if no action is taken. 5. **Keep Copies of All Correspondence** – Store them in a safe place (digital or physical). 6. **Seek Help Early** – Contact local tenant‑rights groups, the TDHCA, or an attorney if you face eviction or serious habitability issues. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Tenant‑landlord dispute resolution, housing assistance, and enforcement of housing codes. | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Handles discrimination complaints. | https://www.tchr.texas.gov | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Federal fair housing enforcement. | https://www.hud.gov | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free legal clinics, mediation services, and educational workshops. | Search online for “tenant rights Texas” + your city. | | **Texas Property Code** | Statutory text governing landlord‑tenant relationships. | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/PC/htm/PC.92.htm | --- #### When to Call an Attorney - **Unlawful Eviction**: If you receive an eviction notice but have paid rent or the landlord has breached the lease. - **Security Deposit Dispute**: If the landlord refuses to return your deposit or provides insufficient justification. - **Habitability Violations**: If major repairs are ignored and the property becomes unsafe. - **Discrimination Claims**: If you suspect the landlord is treating you unfairly based on protected characteristics. --- **Bottom Line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment, and a clear process for rent increases and evictions. By staying informed, documenting everything, and knowing where to seek help, you can protect your rights and address problems effectively.
